analogy.p: Picture **diamond** as a **climbing frame made of steel bars**, with every joint connected to four others in every direction: it cannot bend or slide, so it is hard and rigid. **Graphite** is like a **stack of mesh sheets** or a deck of cards: each sheet is strongly woven but sheets only weakly touch, so they slide over each other easily. Tiny charged 'marbles' (delocalised electrons) can run along the sheets, like marbles rolling on a tray, which is why graphite conducts. **Graphene** is **one sheet** from the stack, and a **nanotube** is that sheet **rolled up**. The analogy breaks down because paper sheets are not bonded atoms: real graphite layers are held by weak forces between electrons and the sheets are only one atom thick, and real electrons are not marbles.
analogy.t: Scaffolding versus a stack of paper

bullets: Describe the **structure** of diamond, graphite, graphene, fullerenes (C60) and nanotubes.
Explain **properties** in terms of **bonding**, for example why graphite conducts and diamond does not.

Know **uses**: diamond for **cutting tools**, graphite as a **lubricant** and for **electrodes**, graphene in **electronics and composites**, nanotubes in **nanotechnology, electronics and materials**, fullerenes for **drug delivery, lubricants and catalysts**.
Compare these with other **giant covalent** structures such as silicon dioxide and with **metals**.
Use diagrams to **recognise** each structure and be able to **draw simple versions**.
Note that fullerenes are **molecules** (simple molecular structures) while diamond and graphite are **giant covalent structures**.
This is a **Paper 1** topic that often appears as a **4 to 6 mark** 'explain why' question.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 8462 section 4.2.3 asks you to describe and explain the **structures and properties of the different forms of carbon**: **diamond, graphite, graphene and the fullerenes** (including **buckminsterfullerene C60** and **carbon nanotubes**). For each one you must know **how the atoms are bonded**, **what the structure looks like**, **why that structure gives the properties** and **what it is used for**. These forms are **allotropes** or related structures of carbon, which means they are made of the same element but arranged differently. The core skill is the examiner's chain: **structure and bonding, then property, then use**.

bullets: Carbon has **atomic number 6** and electronic structure **2,4**, so it needs **four more electrons** to fill its outer shell.
A **covalent bond** is a **shared pair of electrons** between two atoms, and covalent bonds are **strong**.
**Allotropes** are different forms of the **same element** in the same physical state; they have the same atoms but different **structures** and so different **properties**.
In **diamond** each carbon forms **4** covalent bonds; in **graphite, graphene and fullerenes** each carbon forms **3** covalent bonds.
That **fourth electron** in graphite, graphene and fullerenes is **not used for bonding between atoms in the same way**: in graphite and graphene it is **delocalised**.
Everything here is **carbon only**: if a question asks why they differ, the answer is always **different bonding and arrangement**, never different atoms.
These substances are not metals: **graphite is a non-metal that conducts electricity**, which is an unusual property students must explain.
core.h: Carbon atoms, covalent bonding and allotropes
core.p: Carbon is in **Group 4** of the periodic table, so a carbon atom has **four electrons in its outer shell**. To get a full outer shell it **shares electrons** and forms **covalent bonds**. The number of bonds each carbon atom makes and the way they are arranged differ between the forms of carbon, which gives them very different properties even though they contain **only carbon atoms**. Different structural forms of the same element in the same physical state are called **allotropes**; diamond and graphite are the classic examples. Graphene and the fullerenes are related carbon structures built from similar rings of atoms.

bullets: Each carbon atom forms **four covalent bonds** with four other carbon atoms.
The structure is a **giant covalent lattice**: the pattern repeats in three dimensions through millions of atoms.
The structure contains **only strong covalent bonds**; there are **no weak forces** between layers or molecules.
**All four outer electrons** of each carbon are used in bonding, so there are **no delocalised electrons**.
A diamond crystal is effectively **one enormous molecule**, so the formula is simply **C**.
Bond arrangement is **tetrahedral** (higher tier extension) which makes the lattice **rigid**.
Do **not** write 'diamond molecules' or 'diamond has ionic bonding'.
core.p: In **diamond** every carbon atom is joined to **four other carbon atoms by strong covalent bonds**. The bonds are arranged in a rigid three dimensional network that extends throughout the whole crystal, so diamond is called a **giant covalent structure** (or giant covalent lattice). Because every outer electron is used in bonding, there are **no free electrons**. The bonds point in a **tetrahedral** pattern (an extension idea) so the structure is the same strong framework in all directions.

bullets: **Very hard** because each atom is held by **four strong covalent bonds** in a rigid 3D network.
**Very high melting and boiling point** because **a lot of energy** is needed to break the **many strong covalent bonds**.
**Does not conduct electricity** because there are **no delocalised electrons or ions** free to move.
**Insoluble in water** because the strong covalent bonds cannot be separated by solvent molecules.
**Uses**: **cutting tools and drill bits** (diamond-tipped), **glass cutters**, and **jewellery**.
It is also a **good conductor of thermal energy** (an extension fact) but you are rarely asked this in GCSE.
Exam sentence: 'Diamond has a **giant covalent structure** with each carbon forming **four strong covalent bonds**, so it is **very hard**.'
core.p: Each property of diamond comes straight from its structure. Because **every atom is held by four strong covalent bonds in a rigid lattice**, diamond is **extremely hard** (the hardest natural substance). To melt or boil diamond you must **break many strong covalent bonds**, requiring a huge amount of energy, so it has a **very high melting point** (above 3500 °C). With **no delocalised electrons or ions**, there are no charged particles free to move, so diamond **does not conduct electricity**. These properties make it ideal for **cutting and drilling**, while its sparkle and hardness make it valuable in **jewellery**.

bullets: Each carbon atom forms **three covalent bonds** with three other carbon atoms.
The atoms are arranged in **hexagonal rings** forming **flat layers** (like a honeycomb or chicken wire).
There are **no covalent bonds between the layers**; only **weak forces of attraction** hold the layers together.
**One electron per carbon atom** is **delocalised** and can move through the layer.
Graphite is a **giant covalent structure** with a **layered** shape.
The distance between layers is much **larger** than the distance between atoms in a layer, showing that the layers are **weakly held**.
Graphite is **not a metal** but has **metal-like electrical conductivity** because of its delocalised electrons.
core.p: In **graphite** each carbon atom is bonded to only **three other carbon atoms** by strong covalent bonds. These bonds link the atoms into flat **layers of hexagonal rings**. There are **no covalent bonds between the layers**; instead the layers are held together by **weak forces** (called intermolecular forces in the AQA mark scheme). Each carbon atom has **one electron that is not used in bonding**, and this electron is **delocalised**: it is free to move along the layer. Graphite is therefore a giant covalent structure that has **layers** and **delocalised electrons**.

bullets: **Soft and slippery**: **weak forces between layers** let them **slide over each other**.
**High melting point**: **strong covalent bonds** within layers must be broken, which needs **a lot of energy**.
**Conducts electricity**: **one delocalised electron per carbon atom** can move through the structure and carry charge.
**Conducts heat**: delocalised electrons transfer thermal energy.
**Insoluble in water** and **less dense than diamond** because the layers are spaced out.
**Opaque and black/grey and shiny**, unlike diamond which is transparent.
**Higher tier extension**: graphite conducts well **along the layers** but poorly **between layers**.
Compare: **diamond** has **four bonds per carbon**, no delocalised electrons; **graphite** has **three bonds per carbon**, one delocalised electron.
core.p: Graphite's strange mixture of properties comes from its two types of force: **strong covalent bonds within layers** and **weak forces between layers**. Because the layers are only weakly held, they can **slide over each other easily**, so graphite is **soft and slippery**. Because the covalent bonds within the layers are very strong, a lot of energy is needed to break them, so graphite has a **very high melting point**. The **delocalised electrons** can move along the layers carrying charge, so graphite **conducts electricity** (and also conducts thermal energy). This is the combination examiners love to ask: 'Explain why graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not.'

bullets: **Lubricant**: **layers slide over each other** because of **weak forces between layers**.
**Electrodes** (for example in **electrolysis**): **conducts electricity**, has a **very high melting point** and is **unreactive** (inert) so does not react with the products.
**Pencils**: layers **rub off** onto paper (the 'lead' is graphite and clay).
Exam trap: do not give a use without a reason; say '**because** the layers can slide'.
Link: **electrolysis** in 4.4 uses **graphite (inert) electrodes** because they conduct and do not react.
core.p: The uses of graphite follow directly from its properties. Because the layers slide easily, graphite is used as a **lubricant**, for instance in machinery or in lock mechanisms where oils would be unsuitable, and in **pencils** where layers rub off onto paper. Because it **conducts electricity** and has a **high melting point** and is **unreactive**, it is used to make **electrodes** for electrolysis (for example in extracting aluminium and in the electrolysis of brine). Lubricant and electrode uses are the standard exam answers and you must link each to a property.

bullets: Graphene is **one layer of graphite**: a **two dimensional** sheet of hexagonal rings of carbon atoms.
It is **one atom thick**, which makes it **very light** and almost **transparent**.
It is **very strong** because of the **strong covalent bonds** between carbon atoms in the sheet.
It **conducts electricity** because each carbon has **one delocalised electron** which can move across the sheet.
**Uses**: **electronics** (for example flexible displays and fast transistors) and **composites** to make materials **stronger and lighter**.
**Not a molecule**: graphene is a **giant covalent** layer.
Do not say 'graphene is stronger than diamond' as a fact: say **very strong**.
Higher tier thinking: its properties let engineers use **very little material** for a large effect.
core.p: **Graphene** is a **single layer of graphite**, a sheet of carbon atoms joined in **hexagonal rings** that is **only one atom thick**. Each carbon atom is bonded to **three others** by strong covalent bonds and has **one delocalised electron**, so graphene **conducts electricity**. Because the covalent bonds are so strong, graphene is **very strong** for its thickness, yet it is also **very light** because it is only one atom thick. These properties make graphene extremely useful in **electronics** and in **composites** (materials made of two or more substances which are combined to give improved properties).

bullets: Fullerenes are **molecules of carbon**: **hollow spheres or tubes**.
They are **based on hexagonal rings**, but may also contain **pentagons (5 carbons) or heptagons (7 carbons)**.
The **pentagons and heptagons** let the structure **curve**: a flat sheet of only hexagons cannot form a ball.
Fullerenes have **several uses**: **drug delivery** (they can carry a drug inside the cage), **lubricants**, **catalysts** and **reinforcing materials** (for example in sports equipment).
Each carbon is bonded to **three** other carbons, as in graphene.
They are **molecular**, so they are held to each other by **weak intermolecular forces** and are **softer** with **lower melting points** than diamond or graphite.
Family includes **C60**, other **spheres** and **nanotubes**.
core.p: **Fullerenes** are **molecules of carbon** shaped like **hollow tubes or closed cages (spheres)**. Their structure is based on **hexagonal rings of carbon atoms**, but they can also contain rings with **five or seven carbon atoms**, which is what allows the flat hexagonal pattern to curve into a hollow shape. Fullerenes are **simple molecular** (they are discrete molecules), which is different from diamond and graphite, which are giant structures. The first fullerene discovered was **buckminsterfullerene (C60)**, which has a **spherical** shape.

bullets: Formula **C60**: **60 carbon atoms** per molecule, **spherical** shape.
Made of **20 hexagonal** and **12 pentagonal** rings (a football pattern).
**Relative formula mass (Mr)** = 60 × 12 = **720**.
**Simple molecular**: **weak intermolecular forces** between molecules means **less energy** is needed to separate them.
**Hollow** so it can **carry a drug** or other molecule inside (drug delivery).
Uses studied include **drug delivery**, **lubricants** and **catalysts**; a lubricant works because the separate molecules are only weakly attracted to each other.
Discovery: named after the architect **Buckminster Fuller** whose domes it resembles.
Common misconception: 'C60 has 60 bonds'. It has **60 atoms** and **90 bonds** (a higher tier extension count).
core.p: **Buckminsterfullerene** has the formula **C60**: each molecule contains **60 carbon atoms** arranged as a hollow ball made of **20 hexagons and 12 pentagons**, like a football. It was the **first fullerene to be discovered**. Because it is a **simple molecule**, the forces between molecules are **weak intermolecular forces**, so **C60 solid is soft and has a much lower melting point than diamond or graphite**. Its hollow cage can **trap other atoms or molecules**, which is why it is researched for **drug delivery**.

bullets: Nanotubes are **cylindrical** fullerenes with a **very high length to diameter ratio**.
**High tensile strength**: they can be **stretched without breaking**, because of the many **strong covalent bonds**.
**Conduct electricity** because of **delocalised electrons**.
**Uses**: **nanotechnology**, **electronics**, **reinforcing materials** (for example in tennis rackets).
A nanotube has a diameter of a few **nanometres** (1 nm = 1 × 10^-9 m); this links to **nanoparticles** later in the topic.
Nanotubes are **not a giant lattice**: they are long molecules, but so long that they behave like fibres.
Link: **graphene sheet rolled into a cylinder** gives the idea of how the tube relates to graphite.
core.p: **Carbon nanotubes** are **cylindrical fullerenes**: a sheet of hexagonally arranged carbon atoms rolled into a **tube** with a very small diameter, a few nanometres across, but a much greater length. They have a **very high length to diameter ratio**. Because the covalent bonds along the tube are strong and each carbon atom has a delocalised electron, nanotubes are **very strong, light** and **conduct electricity** and thermal energy. Their properties make them useful in **nanotechnology, electronics and materials**, for example as **reinforcement in sports equipment** and as **tiny wires** in circuits.

bullets: **Bonds per carbon**: diamond **4**; graphite, graphene and fullerenes **3**.
**Structure**: diamond **giant covalent lattice**; graphite **giant layered structure**; graphene **single layer**; fullerenes **simple molecules**.
**Conducts electricity**: diamond **no**; graphite **yes**; graphene **yes**; nanotubes **yes**.
**Hardness**: diamond **very hard**; graphite **soft**; graphene **very strong**; C60 solid **soft**.
**Melting point**: diamond and graphite **very high**; fullerenes (simple molecular) **much lower**.
**Uses**: diamond **cutting**; graphite **lubricant, electrodes**; graphene **electronics**; nanotubes **materials**; C60 **drug delivery**.
Quick test: **'conducts + layers'** points to graphite; **'hardest + no conductor'** points to diamond.
core.p: Examiners often give you a table or a list of properties and ask you to identify which carbon structure fits, so you should be able to **compare all four systematically**: **bonds per carbon, structure type, electrical conductivity, hardness and a use**. The key differences are that **diamond** has four bonds per carbon and no delocalised electrons; **graphite** has three bonds per carbon and layers held by weak forces; **graphene** is a single layer; and **fullerenes** are molecules (balls or tubes) with weak forces between the molecules.

bullets: **Silicon dioxide**: giant covalent, very hard, very high melting point, does not conduct: **like diamond**.
**Metals**: delocalised electrons and sliding layers: **like graphite** in conductivity.
**Ionic compounds**: conduct only when **molten or dissolved**, unlike graphite which conducts as a solid.
**Simple molecules**: weak **intermolecular forces** and low melting points: **like fullerenes**.
All **allotropes** of carbon are **non-metal elements** but graphite is the **best-known non-metal that conducts** electricity well.
Link: **electrolysis** uses graphite electrodes; **polymers** are also carbon-based.
core.h: Linking to silicon dioxide, metals and bonding
core.p: Carbon structures sit alongside other bonding types you have studied. **Silicon dioxide** is another giant covalent structure like diamond (no delocalised electrons, very high melting point, hard, does not conduct). **Metals** also conduct because of delocalised electrons, and metals have layers that can slide, so graphite resembles a metal in some ways. The difference is that in graphite the layers slide because they are held only by weak forces, and the delocalised electrons are within each layer. In **simple molecular** fullerenes, like other small molecules, the weak forces between molecules explain the lower melting points.

bullets: **Template (hardness)**: 'giant covalent structure, each C forms 4 strong covalent bonds, rigid, so very hard'.
**Template (conductivity)**: 'delocalised electrons are free to move and carry charge, so it conducts'.
**Template (soft)**: 'layers held by weak forces so layers slide over each other'.
**Template (melting point)**: 'a lot of energy needed to break strong covalent bonds'.
Use **comparison words**: whereas, but, in contrast.
Do not say 'it has free electrons' for diamond; say **'no delocalised electrons'**.
Do not say 'graphite has ionic bonding' or 'metallic bonding'.
core.p: Most marks on this topic are won by following a **structure, bonding, property** chain and by using precise words. Start with the **type of structure**, give the **number of bonds** per carbon, say whether there are **delocalised electrons** or **weak forces**, and then state the **consequence for the property**. Never write the property without a reason, and never mix up **intermolecular forces** (weak, between layers or molecules) with **covalent bonds** (strong, inside layers or molecules).

exam: **1 mark** questions: name the carbon structure from a diagram or description, or state one use.
**2 mark** questions: 'Give a use and a reason': 'graphite as a lubricant (1) because the layers slide over each other (1)'.

**3 to 4 mark 'explain why graphite conducts but diamond does not'**: graphite has **delocalised electrons** (1) that **move** and carry charge (1); diamond has **no delocalised electrons** (1) as all outer electrons are in **covalent bonds** (1).
**'Explain why diamond is hard'**: 'giant covalent structure; each carbon forms **4 strong covalent bonds**; **a lot of energy** needed to break them'.
**'Explain why graphite is soft'**: **layers** (1), **weak forces between layers** (1), **layers slide** (1).
**6 mark comparison**: structure (bonds per carbon), delocalised electrons, hardness, melting point, a use for each; finish with a **conclusion linking structure to property**.
**Diagram questions**: identify graphite by **layers of hexagons**, diamond by **each atom with four bonds**, C60 by a **hollow ball**, nanotube by a **cylinder**.
**Fullerene uses**: drug delivery, lubricants, catalysts, reinforcing materials; **nanotubes**: electronics, nanotechnology, strong materials.
**Maths**: relative formula mass of C60 = 60 × 12 = **720**; check units and show working.
Use the word **'delocalised'** exactly; 'free electrons' is also accepted by AQA but 'delocalised' is safest.
Never say 'molecules' for diamond or graphite; say **giant covalent structure**.

mistakes.r: Graphite conducts because each carbon has one delocalised electron that is free to move along the layers.
mistakes.w: Graphite conducts electricity because it has free ions or metallic bonding.

mistakes.r: The covalent bonds in the layers are strong; it is soft because the weak forces between the layers let the layers slide.
mistakes.w: Graphite is soft because its covalent bonds are weak.

mistakes.r: Diamond has no molecules; a lot of energy is needed to break the many strong covalent bonds in the giant lattice.
mistakes.w: Diamond has a high melting point because of strong intermolecular forces / strong forces between molecules.

mistakes.r: Diamond has no delocalised (free) electrons: all four outer electrons are used in covalent bonds.
mistakes.w: Diamond does not conduct because it has no electrons.

mistakes.r: Graphene is a giant covalent layer, whereas fullerenes such as C60 are simple molecules.
mistakes.w: Graphene is a molecule / C60 is a giant structure.

mistakes.r: Fullerenes contain hexagons but also pentagons (or heptagons), which allow the structure to curve into a ball or tube.
mistakes.w: Fullerenes are made only of hexagons.

mistakes.r: Graphite has 3 covalent bonds per carbon (one electron is delocalised); diamond has 4.
mistakes.w: Graphite has 4 bonds per carbon like diamond.

mistakes.r: Graphite is a lubricant because its layers can slide over each other (weak forces between layers).
mistakes.w: Graphite is used as a lubricant because it is hard.

mistakes.r: No covalent bonds break; only weak forces between layers are overcome.

summary: The specification asks you to describe the structures of diamond, graphite, graphene, fullerenes (including buckminsterfullerene C60) and carbon nanotubes, and explain their properties (hardness, melting point, electrical conductivity, slipperiness) and uses in terms of bonding, covalent bonds per carbon, delocalised electrons and weak forces between layers or molecules. It matters because it is a favourite long-answer topic on Paper 1.

terms.d: Different forms of the same element in the same physical state, with atoms bonded in different arrangements.
A structure in which very many atoms are joined by strong covalent bonds in a continuous network.
A strong bond formed when a pair of electrons is shared between two atoms.
An allotrope of carbon in which each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds in a giant rigid lattice.
An allotrope of carbon in which each carbon forms three covalent bonds to make layers of hexagonal rings with weak forces between the layers.
An electron that is not attached to one atom and is free to move through the structure, so it can carry charge.
Rings of six carbon atoms; the basic repeating unit in graphite, graphene and fullerenes.
A single layer of graphite, one atom thick, made of hexagonal rings of carbon atoms.
A molecule of carbon shaped like a hollow tube or closed cage, based on hexagonal rings and may include rings of five or seven carbon atoms.
The first fullerene discovered; a spherical molecule of 60 carbon atoms.
A cylindrical fullerene with a very high length to diameter ratio.
Weak forces of attraction between molecules (or between layers in graphite) that are easily overcome.
A substance that reduces friction between moving surfaces, for example graphite because its layers slide.
The ability of a material to resist being pulled apart without breaking.
A material made of two or more different substances combined to give improved properties.
The use of structures that are between 1 and 100 nanometres in size.

worked.ans: In graphite each carbon atom forms three covalent bonds, leaving one electron per atom delocalised. These delocalised electrons are free to move through the layers and carry electric charge, so graphite conducts electricity. In diamond each carbon forms four covalent bonds, using all of its outer electrons, so there are no delocalised electrons (or ions) that are free to move, and diamond does not conduct.
worked.q: Explain why graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not. [4 marks]
steps: Say how many bonds each carbon forms: graphite 3, diamond 4.
Graphite: one electron per carbon is not used in bonding, so it is delocalised and can move along the layers.
Delocalised electrons carry charge, so graphite conducts.
Diamond: all four outer electrons form covalent bonds, so there are no delocalised electrons or ions to carry charge.

worked.ans: As a lubricant: graphite has layers with only weak forces between them, so the layers slide over each other easily. As an electrode: graphite has delocalised electrons which carry charge so it conducts electricity, and it has a very high melting point because it has strong covalent bonds, so it does not melt in electrolysis.
worked.q: Graphite is used as a lubricant and for electrodes. Explain why graphite is suitable for each use. [4 marks]
steps: Lubricant: graphite has layers held by weak forces.
The layers can slide over each other easily, so it reduces friction.
Electrodes: delocalised electrons carry current, so it conducts.
It has a very high melting point and is unreactive (strong covalent bonds), so it does not melt or react in electrolysis.

worked.ans: (a) Mr = 720. (b) 0.005 mol of C60 contains 0.30 mol of carbon atoms.
worked.q: Calculate (a) the relative formula mass of buckminsterfullerene, C60 (Ar of C = 12), and (b) the number of moles of carbon atoms in 3.6 g of C60. [3 marks]
steps: (b) Moles of C60 = mass / Mr = 3.6 / 720 = 0.005 mol.
Each molecule has 60 carbon atoms, so moles of carbon atoms = 0.005 × 60 = 0.30 mol.
Check: 3.6 g of carbon atoms / 12 = 0.30 mol, which matches.
